course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Cold War and Decolonization
unit.description: Study how the Cold War divided the world, how colonies won independence, how new states and movements challenged established power, and why the Cold War ended.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: John F. Kennedy, president of the United States, inaugural address, January 20, 1961
stimulusBlocks.citation: John F. Kennedy, Inaugural Address, January 20, 1961. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (inaugural/1961-Kennedy.txt).
stimulusBlocks.note: “New States” are countries that had recently won independence from colonial rule; seventeen African colonies became independent in 1960 alone. “The deadly atom” refers to nuclear weapons.
stimulusBlocks.text:
Let every nation know, whether it wishes us well or ill, that we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship, support any friend, oppose any foe, in order to assure the survival and the success of liberty. . . .

To those new States whom we welcome to the ranks of the free, we pledge our word that one form of colonial control shall not have passed away merely to be replaced by a far more iron tyranny. We shall not always expect to find them supporting our view. . . .

But neither can two great and powerful groups of nations take comfort from our present course -- both sides overburdened by the cost of modern weapons, both rightly alarmed by the steady spread of the deadly atom, yet both racing to alter that uncertain balance of terror that stays the hand of mankind's final war.

questions.prompt: In the third paragraph, Kennedy argues that
choices: the United States should end its alliances

nuclear weapons made the world safer
only the Soviet Union was building weapons
questions.explanation: He describes both sides as overburdened and alarmed.
choiceExplanations: He pledges to support friends.
He describes both sides as overburdened and alarmed.
He calls the balance uncertain.
He says “both racing.”
questions.distinguisher: Kennedy says the balance holds off war but calls it an “uncertain balance of terror.”

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 8.3 key concept: the superpowers supported opposing sides in proxy wars in Asia, Africa, and Latin America
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing Cold War proxy wars, 1950–1989
stimulusBlocks.text:
The superpowers never fought each other directly, but they backed opposing sides in wars around the world. In Korea from 1950 to 1953, a US-led United Nations force fought North Korean and Chinese troops supplied by the Soviet Union. The war ended near where it began, along the 38th parallel.

In Angola after independence in 1975, a government backed by the Soviet Union and thousands of Cuban troops fought rebels supported by the United States and South Africa. In Afghanistan from 1979 to 1989, Soviet troops fought Islamic guerrillas armed by the United States through Pakistan.

questions.prompt: The conflicts in Angola and Afghanistan described in the passage were similar in that
choices: both ended with Soviet victory
the superpowers backed opposing sides
both were fought in Latin America
the United States sent its own troops to both
questions.explanation: In each case one superpower backed the government and the other backed rebels.
choiceExplanations: Soviet troops withdrew from Afghanistan in 1989.
In each case one superpower backed the government and the other backed rebels.
Angola is in Africa and Afghanistan in Asia.
The United States armed others rather than sending troops.
questions.distinguisher: The United States supplied weapons to local forces in both wars, without sending its army.

questions.prompt: Which detail shows that both superpowers made concessions to end the crisis?
choices: Khrushchev agreed to remove missiles and the United States agreed to nothing
The United States promised not to invade Cuba and removed its Turkish missiles
The United States removed its navy from the Caribbean while Soviet missiles stayed
The superpowers agreed to destroy all of their nuclear weapons
questions.explanation: Each side gave something: the Soviets withdrew missiles and the Americans promised not to invade Cuba and removed missiles from Turkey.
choiceExplanations: The passage describes American promises in exchange.
Each side gave something: the Soviets withdrew missiles and the Americans promised not to invade Cuba and removed missiles from Turkey.
The passage says the missiles were removed.
The passage does not describe full nuclear disarmament.
questions.distinguisher: Khrushchev did remove the missiles, but the passage shows the United States also made commitments.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 8.3 key concept: the nuclear arms race and crises such as the Cuban Missile Crisis shaped superpower relations
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Cuban Missile Crisis, October 1962
stimulusBlocks.text:
In October 1962, American reconnaissance photographs showed Soviet nuclear missile sites under construction in Cuba, about 90 miles from Florida. President John F. Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of Cuba and demanded that the missiles be removed. For several days the superpowers came close to nuclear war.

The crisis ended when Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in return for a public American promise not to invade Cuba and a private agreement to remove American missiles from Turkey. In 1963 the two powers installed a telephone hotline between Washington and Moscow and signed a treaty banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere.

questions.prompt: Which long-term result of the crisis is shown in the passage?
choices: A permanent American military base on the island of Cuba
A hotline and test ban to reduce the risk of nuclear war
The end of the arms race between the two superpowers
A Soviet withdrawal from the United Nations in 1963
questions.explanation: In 1963 the powers installed a hotline and signed a treaty banning atmospheric tests.
choiceExplanations: The passage says the United States promised not to invade Cuba.
In 1963 the powers installed a hotline and signed a treaty banning atmospheric tests.
The arms race continued for decades.
The passage does not describe a Soviet withdrawal from the UN.
questions.distinguisher: The test ban was a step toward arms control, but it did not end the arms race.
